title: AI Fundamentals
summary: What AI, machine learning and large language models actually are, in plain language.

lessons.title: AI, ML and deep learning
points: Artificial intelligence (AI) is the broad field of making computers do tasks that normally need human intelligence.
Machine learning (ML) is a type of AI where systems learn patterns from data instead of following hand-written rules.
Deep learning is ML using many-layered neural networks. It powers modern image, speech and language AI.

lessons.title: How a large language model works
points: A large language model (LLM) is trained on huge amounts of text to predict the next token, a word or piece of a word.
By repeatedly predicting the next token, it can answer questions, summarise, translate and write code.
It doesn't look facts up by default. It generates likely-sounding text, which is why it can be wrong.

lessons.title: Training vs. using a model
points: Training: the model learns from data. It's expensive and done in advance by the developer.
Inference: using the trained model to produce an answer, which happens every time you send a prompt.
A model's knowledge stops at its training cut-off unless it's connected to search or documents (retrieval-augmented generation, RAG).

lessons.title: Strengths and limits
points: Great at drafting, summarising, brainstorming, explaining and transforming text or code.
Weak points: hallucinations, outdated knowledge, bias from training data, and inconsistent answers to the same question.
Generative AI creates new content (text, images, audio). Predictive AI classifies or forecasts, like spam filters or fraud scores.

options: Robots that learn to walk only
Systems that learn patterns from data rather than only following hand-written rules
questions.why: ML systems improve at a task by learning from examples in data.

questions.q: At its core, what is a large language model trained to do?
options: Predict the next token in a sequence of text
Store a copy of every website
questions.why: LLMs are trained to predict the next token, and that simple objective at huge scale produces useful language abilities.

questions.q: An LLM always looks up facts in a live database before answering.
questions.why: By default a model generates text from patterns learned in training. Some apps add search or document retrieval, but the base model doesn't.

options: Confident, plausible output that is false or made up
When the AI refuses to answer
questions.why: Models can produce fluent but incorrect answers, including invented sources.

options: Using a trained model to generate an output
questions.why: Inference is running the trained model on new input, which happens every time you send a prompt.

questions.q: A model's built-in knowledge generally stops at its training cut-off date.
questions.why: Unless connected to search or documents, a model doesn't know about events after its training data was collected.

options: Fetches relevant documents and gives them to the model as context for its answer
questions.why: RAG retrieves relevant information (e.g. from your documents) and adds it to the prompt so answers can be grounded in it.

questions.q: Which is an example of predictive (not generative) AI?
options: An email spam filter classifying messages
questions.why: Spam filters classify existing items. Generative AI creates new content.

questions.q: Asking an LLM the same question twice can give different answers.
questions.why: Outputs are often sampled with some randomness, so wording and even conclusions can vary.

questions.q: What is a 'token' in the context of LLMs?
options: A chunk of text, such as a word or part of a word, that the model processes
questions.why: Models break text into tokens. Usage limits and pricing are often measured in tokens.
